how-much-do-you-need-to-sell-at-a-craft-.text:
How much do you need to sell at a craft fair to break even?

Not the booth fee. That is the answer most makers carry around, and it is the reason a market that looked like a good day turns out not to have been one.

Why the booth fee is the wrong target

Every dollar that crosses your table arrives with money already spent on it. The materials and packaging in the piece are gone whether you sell it for $38 or $58. If the customer taps a card, the processor takes a percentage and a fixed few cents. What is left over — the contribution — is the only part that can go toward the booth.

So the question is not "what does the booth cost?" but "how many dollars of sales does it take to produce that much contribution?"

The method, in four steps

1. Add up what the day costs before a single sale

Booth or stall fee, the application or jury fee (usually non-refundable, and paid whether or not you got in — so it belongs to the show you did get into), round-trip mileage, lodging if it is a long haul, parking and tolls, and a share of what your tent, tables, racks, and lights cost spread over the events you expect to use them for.

A $250 two-day booth, 90 miles each way at $0.67, one tent amortized
Booth fee$250.00
Application/jury fee$25.00
Mileage, 90 mi @ $0.67$60.30
Parking & tolls$15.00
Tent & display, per event$20.00
Fixed cost of the day$370.30

2. Work out what you keep from each dollar of sales

Subtract your materials-and-packaging percentage, then your card cost. The card cost has two parts and the second one surprises people: the percentage is easy, but the fixed fee per transaction only becomes a rate once you divide it by your average order value.

Materials & packaging30.0c
Card percentage, 2.6% on 80% of sales2.1c
Card fixed fee, 10c per sale on a $38 average0.2c
Kept from each dollar67.7c

That last line is where a sticker table and a print table part company. Ten cents on a $6 sale is 1.7% of it; the same ten cents on an $80 sale is 0.1%. A processor's headline "2.6% + 10c" hides that difference completely.

3. Divide

$370.30 of fixed cost, at 67.7c kept per dollar, needs $546.90 of sales to break even — about 15 orders at a $38 average. Not $370, and not 10 orders.

4. Then decide whether break-even is the bar you meant

Breaking even means the day paid for itself and paid you nothing. Count the hours honestly — making and packing stock for the show, the drive both ways, load-in and teardown, and the hours the booth is open — and put your own number on them. Twenty-six hours at $25 is $650 more that the day has to produce, which moves break-even to about $1,507.

Those two figures answer different questions, and both are worth knowing. The first says whether you lost money. The second says whether you should have gone.

Run it on your own market. The craft fair booth calculator does the arithmetic above from your fees, mileage, materials percentage, average order, and hours — and adds the number an application actually turns on: the most a booth could cost and still clear your hourly rate. Nothing you type leaves your browser.

Why unsold stock is not a cost of the event

This is the correction that changes the most minds, and it is the one that separates a maker's break-even from a caterer's.

A caterer who preps for 150 and serves 90 throws food away: the over-prep is a real loss on that booking. A maker who brings 60 candles and sells 22 drives home with 38 candles. They cost what they cost, but they are still inventory — they sell at the next market, or online, or in December. Charging the whole table's materials against one weekend makes every event look like a disaster until the season is over.

So the materials that belong in one event's arithmetic are the materials in what actually sold. That is why the calculator takes materials as a percentage of retail rather than as a lump, and why the stock figure you enter is used only to express the break-even as a sell-through percentage: what share of the table has to move. If that percentage comes out above 100, the event cannot cover its booth even on a sellout, and the fix is a fuller table or a different show.

Three things this method does not do

  • It does not predict your sales. Nothing can. What it does is turn a sales figure you supply into a decision, and tell you how far off the number would have to be to change that decision.
  • It does not handle sales tax. Tax you collect from a buyer and remit is not revenue; keep it out of the sales figure you enter.
  • It is not a substitute for reading the booth contract. Electricity fees, required insurance certificates, mandatory raffle donations, and commission-on-sales clauses at some juried shows are all real costs — enter them in the other-cost field once you have read for them.

Deciding between shows, not just about one

Once each show is on the same footing, the comparison that matters is not which one sold most — it is which one paid your hours best. A $900 farmers market four miles away with a $40 stall and eight committed hours can beat a $2,000 juried festival with a $600 booth, a hotel, and thirty hours. Run both and compare the hourly line.

The same maker usually sells the same work online between markets. The Etsy profit calculator prices one listing after Etsy's own fees, and the where-to-sell calculator puts one item through every channel at once — useful for the stock that comes home.

Common questions

How much do you need to sell at a craft fair to break even?

More than the booth fee, and usually by a wide margin. Add up everything paid before a single sale — booth fee, application or jury fee, mileage, lodging, parking, and a share of the tent — then work out what you keep from each dollar of sales after materials and card processing. Divide the first by the second. On a $250 booth with a $25 jury fee, 90 miles of driving, 30% materials and a typical card mix, $370.30 of fixed cost at 67.7c kept per dollar needs $546.90 of sales, not $370.

Should I count the stock I did not sell as a loss?

No. It is inventory, not a loss. A caterer who over-preps throws food away, but a maker who brings 60 candles and sells 22 drives home with 38 candles and sells them at the next market or online. The materials that belong in one event's arithmetic are the materials in what actually sold. Charging a whole table against one weekend makes every event look like a disaster until the season is over, and it is the most common reason makers stop applying to shows that were in fact working.

Is a craft fair worth it if I only broke even?

Breaking even means the day paid for itself and paid you nothing. Count the hours honestly — making and packing stock, the drive both ways, load-in and teardown, and the hours the booth is open — and put your own number on them. Twenty-six hours at $25 is $650 the day also has to produce, which moves the bar from $546.90 to about $1,507. Both figures are worth knowing: the first says whether you lost money, the second says whether you should have gone.

Common questions

Why doesn't the stock I don't sell count as a cost of the event?

Because it is still yours. A caterer who over-preps throws food away, but a maker who brings 60 candles and sells 22 drives home with 38 candles and sells them at the next market or online. So the materials that belong in one event's break-even are the materials in what actually sold. Counting the whole table against one weekend is how a fine event gets recorded as a bad one. The stock figure is used only to express the break-even as a sell-through percentage, so you can see what share of the table has to move.

Why is my break-even higher than the booth fee?

Because sales are not profit. Every dollar you take arrives with materials already spent on it and a card fee taken out of it, so only part of each dollar is left to cover the booth. At 30% materials and a card mix around 2.6% plus 10c, roughly 68c of each dollar is available — so a $370 day of fixed cost needs about $547 of sales, not $370. The calculator shows the kept-per-dollar figure it used.

What is the most a booth should cost?

That depends on what you expect to sell there and what you want your own hours to earn. Given both, the calculator solves for the booth fee at which the day lands exactly on your target hourly rate — that is the number to compare against an application before you send it. If it comes out negative, the expected sales cannot clear your target rate even at a free stall, which is a fact about the event's sales rather than about its organiser.

Why does the average order value change the answer so much on cheap items?

Your processor's fixed fee is charged per transaction, not per dollar. Ten cents on a $6 sticker sale is 1.7% of it; the same ten cents on an $80 print is 0.1%. A headline "2.6% + 10c" hides that difference completely, so a sticker table and a print table with identical percentages keep very different shares of each dollar. The calculator converts the fixed fee into a rate using your average order value, which is why that field matters more than it looks.

Does anything about my event or my sales get uploaded?

No. Every field on this page runs in your browser only, there is no account, and nothing you type is uploaded. Nothing leaves this device unless you choose to send it: the Copy shareable link button puts the figures on the form into the page's URL fragment, which a browser never sends to a server or into a Referer header, so it reaches only the person you hand the link to. Anyone who has that link can read the numbers in it, so send it the way you would send the numbers themselves. Usage counting only tallies anonymous feature events, and you can turn it off with the button above.

vs-a-spreadsheet.html.text:
← back to the calculator

Craft fair booth calculator vs a spreadsheet or gut math

Most makers already do a version of this in their head before they apply: sales minus the booth fee. It is fast, and it is wrong in the same direction every time, because it treats the booth fee as the only cost and gross sales as if every dollar of them were kept.

The gut check, and what it leaves out

Sales minus booth feeThis calculator
Materials in what soldNot countedCounted, as a percent of the retail price of what actually sold — not of the whole table brought
Card processingNot countedCounted as both a percentage and a per-transaction fixed fee, converted to a rate using your average order value
Jury fee, mileage, lodging, parking, displayNot counted — only the booth fee isAll counted as fixed cost paid before a single sale
Your own hoursNot counted at allValued at the hourly rate you set, across prep, travel, setup, teardown, and selling
Unsold stockUsually either ignored or, worse, charged whole against the dayLeft out of the event entirely — it is inventory carried to the next show, not a cost of this one

One event, two answers

Take this calculator's own default event: a $250 booth, $25 jury fee, a 90-mile round trip, $1,500 in expected sales, 30% materials, and a mixed cash/card till. The gut check says:

Sales minus booth fee$1,500 − $250 = $1,250 "profit"

Run the same event through every cost actually paid, and the answer looks nothing like that:

Fixed cost paid before any sale (booth, jury fee, mileage, parking, display)$370.30
Materials and card fees out of $1,500 in sales$854.66
Cash left over$645.34
26 committed hours (prep, travel, setup/teardown, selling) at $25/hr$650.00
Left after paying yourself−$4.66

The day still clears its bills by a wide margin, which is exactly the kind of result a "sales minus booth fee" gut check reads as a clear win. Once the maker's own time is priced at a modest $25 an hour, the same day comes out four dollars and change short of that rate. Neither number is wrong — they answer different questions — but only one of them is the one a spreadsheet line usually shows.

Where a spreadsheet gets unsold stock backwards

The other place a quick spreadsheet goes wrong is unsold stock, and it goes wrong in either direction. Some makers ignore it entirely, which silently overstates how much the event actually cost to attend if a large share of the table came home. Others swing the other way and charge the whole table's materials against one weekend, which is how a perfectly fine market gets recorded as a loss — the candles that did not sell are still in the van, not gone. This calculator asks what you are bringing at retail only to report the break-even as a sell-through percentage, so you can see what share of the table has to move without charging the unsold remainder against the day at all.

Run your own numbers. Open the calculator — no account, no upload, nothing kept. Or start with the method: how much you need to sell at a craft fair to break even.

Common questions

What does "sales minus booth fee" get wrong?

It counts gross sales as if every dollar were kept. In reality, materials already spent on what sold and the card processor's cut both come out of that dollar before anything is left, and the booth fee is only one of several costs paid before a single sale — the jury fee, mileage, lodging, parking, and display all belong in the same bucket. A quick mental subtraction misses all of that, and it counts none of the maker's own hours at all.

Why does a spreadsheet total still miss the real answer?

A one-line spreadsheet usually stops at cash left over, which answers whether the day covered its bills but not whether it paid the maker anything for their time. On this calculator's own default event, cash left over is $645.34 — a day that looks clearly profitable — but once prep, travel, setup, teardown, and selling hours are valued at even a modest $25/hour, the day actually falls $4.66 short of that rate. A spreadsheet that never enters an hourly figure cannot show that.

Why does a per-transaction card fee matter more than the percentage suggests?

A processor's fixed fee is charged per sale, not per dollar, so it only becomes a rate once divided by what a typical sale is worth. Ten cents on a $6 sticker is a much bigger bite than ten cents on an $80 print, and a headline "2.6% + 10c" hides that difference completely — a spreadsheet with one blended fee percentage cannot see it either, unless it is built to divide the fixed fee by the average order value the way this calculator does.

Does this calculator store or upload anything I type?

No. Every field runs in your browser and nothing survives closing the tab. The only way figures leave the device is the shareable link you choose to copy, which carries them in the URL fragment — a part of the address a browser never sends to a server.

Craft fair booth calculator vs Craftybase

Not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Craftybase. Craftybase is a trademark of its owner, named here only to describe what this tool is and is not.

These get compared because they are both aimed at makers who sell what they make, and both talk about cost of goods. They answer different questions, and the honest way to choose is to notice which question you actually started with.

What each one is

CraftybaseThis calculator
What it isA paid subscription web application for handmade-business inventory and manufacturing bookkeeping, per its own product pages.A single free web page that runs entirely in your browser.
The question it answersWhat did I make, what did it cost me, what stock do I hold, and what are my numbers at tax time?Is this one market worth taking, what does it have to sell, and what does the weekend pay me per hour?
Time horizonOngoing — it is a system of record you keep up to date.One event, decided in a couple of minutes.
What you enterMaterials, recipes, purchases, and sales, kept current over time.Twenty figures about one show, typed once.
Where the data livesIn your account on their service.Only in your browser tab. There is no account and nothing is uploaded.
CostPaid, on published subscription tiers.Free, with no paid tier and nothing withheld.

When each is the right answer

Reach for real inventory bookkeeping when you need to know your true cost of goods across a whole catalogue, track raw materials down to the yard and the gram, produce accurate numbers for a tax return, or hold stock levels you cannot keep in your head. A one-page calculator is not a system of record and does not pretend to be — this one keeps nothing at all when you close the tab, which is a deliberate privacy choice and a genuine limitation.

Reach for this calculator when an application is open, the booth fee is $250, the drive is ninety miles, and you have a week to decide. It needs no account and no history: you supply a materials percentage and an average order value, and it returns the sales the day has to make, the share of your table that represents, the hourly rate your expected take actually works out to, and the highest booth fee that would still clear the rate you want for your own hours.

They also compose. A maker who tracks cost of goods properly already knows their materials percentage to a point or two, which is the one input here that most people are guessing at — so good bookkeeping makes this page's answer sharper, not redundant.

The one thing this page does that a ledger does not

Bookkeeping is retrospective by nature: it tells you what a show did after you did it. The decision you are making is prospective — whether to send the application at all. Those need different arithmetic, and in particular they treat unsold stock differently.

Inventory accounting is right to carry unsold stock at cost on your books. This page is right to leave it out of one event's break-even entirely, because the candles you drive home are still yours to sell. Charging a whole table's materials against a single weekend is how a perfectly reasonable market gets written off as a bad one, and it is the most common arithmetic mistake makers report about show season.

Try the free calculator. Open it here — no account, no upload, nothing kept. Or read the method first: how much you need to sell at a craft fair to break even.

Common questions

Do I need inventory software to work out whether a craft fair was worth it?

No. The go/no-go on one booth needs six things — the fixed cost of getting there, your materials as a share of retail, your card rate, your average order value, the hours you will commit, and the sales you expect — and none of them requires a system of record. Inventory software answers a different and larger question: what your whole catalogue costs to make and what stock you hold. If you already track that properly you will know your materials percentage precisely, which makes this calculator's answer sharper.

Can I use both?

Yes, and they compose well. Bookkeeping is retrospective by nature: it tells you what a show did after you did it. Deciding whether to send the application is prospective, and needs different arithmetic — in particular it leaves unsold stock out of the event entirely, because the pieces you drive home are still yours to sell. Inventory accounting is right to carry that stock at cost on your books; a single event's break-even is right to ignore it.

Does this calculator store my numbers anywhere?

No. There is no account and nothing is uploaded. Every field runs in your browser and nothing survives closing the tab. That is a deliberate privacy choice and also a genuine limitation: this page is not a system of record and does not pretend to be one. The only way figures leave the device is the shareable link you choose to copy, which carries them in the URL fragment — a part of the address a browser never sends to a server.
